title: Why Museums Matter for Mental Health and Well-Being
content:
Doctors are prescribing gallery visits. Care homes are receiving museum collections. People living with dementia are reliving Eurovision classics with a mobile museum. Here is why museums have become some of the most powerful wellbeing spaces we have.

Most of us who work in museums have felt it. A visitor lingers in front of a painting and leaves looking lighter. A regular at the Tuesday tour turns out to have no one else to talk to all week. A family member tells you their mother, who rarely speaks now, lit up at the sight of an old tin toy.

For a long time, these moments were treated as pleasant side effects. That is changing fast. As health systems strain under rising demand for mental health support, and as loneliness is increasingly recognised as a public health issue in its own right, museums are stepping forward as genuine partners in care.

title: Museums and Climate: Why Cultural Institutions Belong in the Conversation
content:
From exhibitions that turn industrial heritage into hope to galleries built for climate grief, museums are finding their voice on the defining issue of our time. Here is why they belong at the centre of the conversation.

Climate change is often discussed in the language of data: parts per million, degrees of warming, emissions targets. The numbers matter, but they rarely move people. What moves people is story, place, emotion and community, and those are exactly the things museums do best.

Museums also hold a rare position of public trust. They are places where people of every age and background come to make sense of the world, and they can host difficult conversations without the heat of a political debate. That makes them uniquely placed to help the public understand the climate crisis, cope with how it makes them feel, and believe they can do something about it.

And museums are not just commentators. Their buildings, exhibitions and supply chains carry a real environmental footprint, which gives them the chance to lead by example. Here are four ways museums around the world are proving that cultural institutions belong in the climate conversation.

title: Why Museums Matter for Young People
content:
Teenagers are swapping phone numbers at the end of a museum workshop. A young person who barely left home for three years is pitching their own exhibition to journalists. High school students in Los Angeles are teaching their younger siblings breathing exercises they first learned in front of a Van Gogh. Here is why museums matter for young people, and why they matter now more than ever.

Ask most people who museums are for, and young people tend to appear in only two roles: the primary school group on a trip, or the child in a buggy on a family day out. Somewhere between those early visits and adulthood, many of them drift away. The teenage and young adult years are often the point when museums lose them.

Yet these are exactly the years when young people most need what museums quietly offer. Anxiety, loneliness and uncertainty about the future are shaping a generation, and the places that traditionally support young people, from schools to youth services, are under strain. Many young people spend their days being measured, graded and compared, online and off.

title: From Tagging to Togetherness: How Art UK Turned a Digital Tool into Real-World Connection
content:
A simple artwork-tagging tool has become the starting point for friendships, wellbeing and a renewed pride in place. At the Digital Collections Summit, Art UK’s Katey Goodwin and Natalie Willatt explained how.

Digital collections work is often measured in records, clicks and page views. But what happens when a national online platform is deliberately turned into something local, social and face-to-face?

That was the question behind a talk at the Digital Collections Summit by Katey Goodwin, Deputy Chief Executive and Director of Community Engagement at Art UK, and Natalie Willatt, the organisation’s Community Volunteer Manager. Using Art UK’s community volunteering programme in Stoke-on-Trent as a case study, they showed how a crowdsourcing tool called Tagger has sparked genuine human connection, reduced isolation and strengthened people’s relationship with art and place.

As Goodwin put it, Art UK’s mission is simple: to connect people with art. This programme set out to test whether art could also become a catalyst for connecting people with one another.

title: What Will the Future Remember? Why Museums Must Start Collecting Social Media Now
content:
Try to imagine studying the Renaissance without its art. Now imagine a historian in 2126 trying to understand our era without hashtags, viral videos or online activism. At the Digital Collections Summit, Craig Middleton (State Library of South Australia) and Caroline Wilson-Barnao (University of Queensland) argued that museums can no longer afford to leave social media out of their collections, and offered a practical roadmap for getting started.

Here’s a thought experiment worth sitting with. A historian 100 years from now wants to understand what it was like to be alive in 2026. What should they be able to see?

Our buildings, newspapers, government records and photographs, certainly. But what about the TikToks, Instagram posts, Facebook groups, memes, WhatsApp conversations and YouTube videos through which so much of contemporary life is actually lived?

For Middleton and Wilson-Barnao, co-authors of Collecting Social Media in Museums (Routledge, 2025), the answer is an obvious yes. The more interesting question is why so many museums are still hesitant to act on it.

title: How museums can adapt their content to short-video formats
content:
For a growing share of your potential audience, the first encounter with your museum is a vertical video they did not go looking for. It arrives between a recipe and a dog, it lasts forty seconds, and it decides whether they ever think about you again.

Vertical video is now the default unit of social media. TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, Facebook, LinkedIn, Threads and X all push it, and all of them reward organisations that make it natively rather than repurposing whatever the marketing team already had. The question is no longer whether to make short video. It is how to make it well without a production budget you don’t have.

title: One object, one iPhone, one afternoon: How London Museum went viral
content:
Helen Maher and Xuxa Kidd told the Museums & Social Media Summit how a muddy knitted cap pulled from the Thames became their most successful piece of social content.

There is a particular kind of dread that settles over a museum when a public claim turns out to be wrong. Something has been announced. Research moves on. The announcement no longer holds. The instinct, almost always, is to say nothing further and hope the record quietly corrects itself.

London Museum did the opposite, and got 1.1 million views for it.

The object at the centre of the story is a knitted cap, pulled from the Thames foreshore by a mudlark named Alessio and reported through the proper channels. Mudlarking, as Helen Maher, the museum’s social media community manager, explained to delegates, sits somewhere between archaeology, history and treasure hunting: when the tide goes out, the river gives up fragments of the city, and permit-holders go looking for them.

title: How Qatar Museums Built an AI Tour That Actually Reaches Visitors
content:
Plenty of museums are experimenting with Artificial Intelligence (AI), but far fewer have progressed past the pilot stage to deliver something visitors actually use.

Qatar Museums (QM) is a rare exception. Its AI Tour is the world’s first national, AI-powered cultural and art tour, marking a significant milestone in cultural innovation. As a nationally backed, app-free platform, it integrates conversational, generative, and personalisation AI to guide visitors through museums, creative hubs, public art, and heritage sites as a single, customisable, connected journey.

Naturally, the team behind this groundbreaking initiative has firm views on exactly why it works. 

Picture the familiar scenario. You arrive in a new city. How do you actually explore its art and culture? You might seek out a museum, hunt for landmarks, or just wander and hope to stumble on something.

title: Infrastructure Before Output: How Museum of Toronto Built a Digital Ecosystem by Doing the Wrong Things First
content:
Most conference talks about digital strategy focus on the answer. The ecosystem is in place, the team is aligned, the numbers look good. At a recent MuseumNext event, Davin Henson of Museum of Toronto offered something different: a candid account of the years between having a digital presence and having a digital ecosystem, including the wrong turns, the misleading metrics, and the sequencing principle that finally made the work hold together.

Henson had spoken at MuseumNext in 2021 and 2022 about content strategy and digital distribution. Those were honest talks, he said, but early-stage ones. This time he told the fuller story, structured as three phases and one principle: infrastructure before output, in that order.

title: When Boxing Gloves Meet Museum Walls
content:
There is often a wide gulf between culture lovers and sports enthusiasts. In Antwerp, a hyperdiverse city where martial arts of every kind are widely practised, many practitioners have never set foot in a museum, and plenty of museum regulars have never set foot in a boxing gym. At MuseumNext, three speakers from the city explained how an exhibition is starting to bridge that divide.

Hélène De Pagie, a programme maker at the MAS (Museum aan de Stroom), was joined on stage by Rachid Atia of the Heritage Lab and Jamal Touala of Sporting A, the city’s sports department. Together they told the story of the Martial Arts exhibition, which has brought fighters, wrestlers and boxers into one of Antwerp’s most prestigious cultural spaces, and museum visitors into a world many of them had never given much thought.
